points: Triage the pipeline first: missing data, schema changes, delayed features
Compare input distributions for data drift and the prediction distribution
Where labels exist, check performance by segment and time for concept drift
Label drift is a change in the base rate
Fix the cheapest cause first; retrain on a recent window or warm start if needed
Validate with a backtest and add telemetry for next time

key_points.base: I'd monitor in layers: system health (latency, errors), data quality, input and prediction drift as
points: Monitor in layers: system health, data quality, input and prediction drift
Add outcome metrics when delayed labels arrive
Track segment-level and fairness metrics
Tie thresholds to impact and require persistence over several days
Page only for actionable issues
Automate retraining a candidate but keep human approval to promote it

key_points.base: I'd measure first: approval and error rates by group (demographic parity, equalized odds), and invol
points: Measure first: approval and error rates by group
Use fairness metrics like demographic parity and equalized odds
Involve legal and compliance; in lending it's regulatory
Removing protected attributes fails when proxies like zip code carry the signal
Audit and constrain proxies, or use fairness-constrained training or thresholds
The accuracy-fairness tradeoff is a business decision: present options and document

key_points.base: Backtest first, then shadow mode: run old and new side by side on live inputs with no user impact. N
points: Backtest first
Run in shadow mode side by side on live inputs with no user impact
Then a canary or segment rollout with one-step rollback
If better only for some segments, consider routing by segment
Monitor long enough for a full business cycle and for labels to arrive

key_points.base: It's a mismatch between the features the model was trained on and the features it receives in produc
points: Skew is a mismatch between training features and features served in production
Often from duplicated logic, like SQL for training and app code for serving
Also from different null or time zone handling, or leaked future data
Prevent with one shared feature definition, such as a feature store
Build training data with point-in-time correct joins
Log served features and compare their distributions with training

key_points.base: Reproducibility means I can recreate a past model and its predictions. I'd version the code (git com
points: Reproducible means you can recreate a past model and its predictions
Version the code, data snapshot, config and environment
Record everything in a model registry linked to the artifact
Seeds help but parallelism, library versions and GPUs add non-determinism
Test that a re-run lands within tolerance
It matters for debugging, audits and trusting version comparisons

key_points.base: I'd profile a request end to end first, because the time often goes to fetching features or network
points: Profile a request end to end first; time often goes to feature fetch or network
Precompute predictions in batch or cache them if freshness allows
Use fewer or cheaper features
Use a smaller model, distillation or quantization
Batch inference requests
Measure accuracy loss against latency and cost gains; pick the cheapest that meets the SLA

key_points.base: Data (covariate) drift: the distribution of inputs shifts, for instance a lending model sees more yo
points: Data drift: the input distribution shifts
Concept drift: the same inputs now lead to different outcomes
Give a concrete example of each
Data drift is visible from inputs with PSI or KS; concept drift needs labels
Data drift hurts only where the model is weak; concept drift always hurts
Handle data drift with segment checks or reweighting; concept drift by retraining

key_points.base: The training set only contains applicants the old model liked, so the new model never learns what ha
points: You only observe outcomes for approved applicants: selection bias
The model never learns about rejected applicants, so it extrapolates
Wrongly rejected good applicants are never discovered; the loop reinforces itself
Approve a small random slice of borderline applicants to get unbiased labels
Use reject inference with caveats and evaluate on the random holdout
Tell the business what's unknowable and what it costs

key_points.base: I'd choose by how fast the world changes versus how costly retraining and validation are. A schedule
points: Decide by how fast the world changes versus the cost of retraining
A schedule is simple and suits gradual drift
A trigger on drift or performance saves cost when changes are irregular
Continuous learning fits fast, low-risk domains but is hardest to control
Always validate against the current model, shadow or canary, with rollback
Start with a schedule plus alerts and adapt

key_points.base: Bin the feature using the training distribution (quantiles for numeric features), compute the propor
points: Bin the feature using training quantiles
Sum (current minus reference) times ln(current over reference) across bins
Rule of thumb: under 0.1 stable, 0.1 to 0.25 moderate, above 0.25 large
Thresholds are heuristics that depend on bins and sample size
PSI misses shifts within bins, is unstable for sparse bins and ignores performance
Combine with KS or Wasserstein, weight by importance, and investigate before retraining

key_points.base: I'd ask what pain we have today: features recomputed by several teams, inconsistent definitions, tra
points: Start from today's pain: recomputed features, inconsistent definitions, skew
A feature store gives shared definitions and point-in-time training data
It also gives consistent online serving
Costs: infrastructure, ownership, backfills and migration
For a few batch models, warehouse tables and shared code are enough
Pilot on one high-value feature set when there are many models or real-time needs

key_points.base: First hour: confirm the drop is real. Has the label or metric definition changed, and how mature are
points: Confirm the drop is real: metric definitions and label maturity
Check upstream: schema, null rates, feature distributions, joins, traffic mix
Slice precision by segment, channel, merchant and time
A sudden step suggests a pipeline change; a gradual slide suggests adapting fraudsters
Tell stakeholders the impact and an interim fix like raising the threshold
Retrain only after diagnosing

key_points.base: I'd define a shared baseline for all models: data freshness and volume, schema and null checks, pred
points: Define a shared baseline for every model
Baseline: freshness, volume, schema, nulls, prediction distribution, latency, errors
Teams add their own business metrics
Severity tiers: page for outages, ticket for degradation, dashboard for the rest
Each alert has an owner and a runbook
Tune thresholds, group alerts and review alert precision to retire noisy ones

key_points.base: First I'd work out what the overrides mean by slicing them by reviewer, case type and model confiden
points: Slice overrides by reviewer, case type and model confidence
Overrides concentrated in a segment suggest the model is wrong there
Overrides from a few reviewers suggest preference or inconsistency
Overrides using information the model lacks suggest a missing feature
Audit a sample against real outcomes to see who is right
Overrides as labels carry reviewer bias; also watch for rubber-stamping
